chapter_theme: The last chapter of the Sivavakkiyam is a catalogue of religious fraud, alchemists, siddhi-showmen, drug-fed kaya-kalpa men, ochre-robed beggars, sacrificers, idol-makers and river-bathers, set against three positive claims: that grace and virtue, not rites, make the beyond; that the householder who feeds the guest and the man who joins a woman are not below the ascetic; and that the world, its lives and true knowledge stand in the five letters, which, chanted with the breath as சிவாயவசி, become a fire with two heads.
structure_note: 1464 to 1467 move from lust to the defence of marriage; 1468 to 1471 concern the siddhar misread as mad, the calm breath and the futility of wandering; 1472 and 1484 bracket the attack on made gods; 1473 to 1481 are the catalogue of frauds; 1482 to 1487 return to idols, rivers and thieves; 1488 closes the work on the mantra.

1464.reading: Lustful men who gaze longingly at the moon face of a beautiful woman smeared with burnt paste, not knowing how to rise and stand firm: do you not know the trickery of the snake that sleeps in the box? If Brahma unties the knot and looks, what way out is there for you?
1464.nuance: The plain reading is a warning against lust, with the woman as the snake in the box, dangerous when opened. The coded reading takes the sleeping snake as the coiled power at the root, which Brahma, the four-faced one placed there in tantric maps, might loose; the verse fits both. சுட்டெரித்த சாந்து is unclear, perhaps lime or burnt sandal paste.

1465.reading: The labour of reciting the Vedas is wasted on this earth! Running league after league, is a puja of love needed? When the Primal Lord who ate the butter is within us, what worthless puja, what Veda is there? Mark it and look within yourselves.
1465.nuance: வெண்ணெய் உண்ட ஆதிநாதன் (the Primal Lord who ate butter) borrows Krishna's epithet for the Lord within, which is unusual in a Saiva poet and shows the verse's indifference to sect. The verse rejects Veda and puja together as outward labour.

1466.reading: Where is the Supreme absent, and where is it present? For sinners without virtue there is no Supreme, and that is the truth; when there are hands and there is wealth and yet no grace, that is a void without the Supreme, a waste hell.
1466.nuance: The verse answers its own question with ethics, not with a body-place: the Supreme is absent wherever virtue (அறம்) and grace-as-compassion (அருள்) are absent. கரம் இருந்தும் பொருள் இருந்தும் names the able and the rich who do not give. சூனியம் here is plain emptiness, not the yogic void.

1467.reading: There is no god on this earth who has not joined a woman's shoulder! When joined to a woman's shoulder, human life flourishes; because Shakti, who is woman, has become bound up with him, the Lord himself took the blue Ganga, who is woman, with delight.
1467.nuance: A defence of marriage and union from theology: if Siva has Shakti and bears the Ganga, the ascetic's horror of women has no divine warrant. The verse makes the household path a flourishing (சிறக்கும்), not a concession.

1468.reading: Souls who cannot tell the siddhar from the petty man! While siddhars are here you count them mad; and if siddhars were here, would a madman stay in the land? The Father's land and this land are all one to them.
1468.nuance: The siddhar is mistaken for a madman (பித்தர்) because he is indifferent to place: the last line says heaven and earth are one to him. Line 3 is a riddle on the pair சித்தர்/பித்தர் and may mean that a true madman would not endure a land where siddhars live.

1469.reading: When life among men on earth is forgotten, in the sky, if you can set right the life-breath made calm, you can see the feet of the stainless one who dances in the hall as king. Mother of the tresses, not a single crookedness can be found in this; it is truth.
1469.nuance: சாந்தனான ஆவியைச் சரிப்படுத்த (to set right the calmed breath) is a breath instruction, and விண்ணிலே (in the sky) may be the inner space at the crown. The verse is addressed to கூந்தலம்மை, the goddess; the oath that nothing in it is crooked is a seal on the teaching.

1470.reading: Hermits who live on the slopes, chewing dry leaves and drinking water! Eating dry leaves the body wastes and anxiety arises; if instead you eat and dress with the guest who comes and enjoy a growing household, the guest who comes becomes the Lord and grants you life: Sivaayame.
1470.nuance: The verse reverses the ascetic hierarchy: the forest hermit's fast breeds சஞ்சலம் (unrest), and the householder's guest is the Lord himself (விருந்தோன் ஈசனாகி). It is the clearest statement in the Sivavakkiyam that the household is a path.

1471.reading: Will those who leave country and land to wander, clearing forest, mound, hill, hollow and forest river, see the Lord's feet? Because your life, leaving the cage, looks only toward the Dancer's town, there is none among them who has gained release and sat in Hara's state.
1471.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are hard: கூடுவிட்டு அகன்று உன் ஆவி may mean the breath that has left the body at death, so that the pilgrim hopes to reach Siva's town only after dying, or the attention that wanders out of the body. On either reading the verse says the wanderer does not reach release.

1472.reading: Gods made of wood and gods made of stone, gods made of palm-leaf and gods made of turmeric, gods made of cloth and gods made of dung: other than the open space there is no other god.
1472.nuance: Six materials in three lines, from carved stone to the dung image of village rites, all levelled together, and then the one positive claim: வெட்டவெளி, the open expanse, is the only god. The verse does not deny God; it denies him a material.

1473.reading: When your body falls ill, you set pongal at the Pidari shrine and offer goat and cock as sacrifice to it; yet, I tell you plainly, the sickness grows, you waste day by day and shrink to a mouse: it is not your family deity that is deforming you.
1473.nuance: The verse's logic is that the sickness is not the deity's doing, so the sacrifice cannot buy it off. நங்கச் சொல்லு (I say it clearly) and மூஞ்சூராய் (like a shrew or mouse) are read tentatively; the last line could also be ironic, 'your clan god will not harm you', said while the man wastes.

1474.reading: Those who out of greed wander wholly intent on cheating and seizing others' property every day, wicked men who make puja, observances and austerities flourish alongside it: it is truth that the seven hells on this earth wait for them.
1474.nuance: The target is not the thief but the pious thief, whose puja and vows (நேமம், நிட்டை) grow with his thefts. எழுநரகு (seven hells) is placed காசினியில், on this earth, which may mean the hells are here.

1475.reading: Fools who with devotion do puja, smear ash and sandal, wear scent and put the black mark on the brow, and wholly practise deceit, lies and rolled-up fraud: your body is only the white dust where a donkey rolled on the threshing floor.
1475.nuance: The sacred ash on the deceiver is matched to the dust on a rolling donkey: same whiteness, same meaning. The verse does not say ash is empty for everyone, only for those whose conduct is fraud.

1476.reading: 'I will do alchemy: silver, and gold finer than the touchstone's gold'; saying 'give gold and coins enough for the guru's bundle', performing tricks and deceiving, they take the property that was handed over and run a league away; even catching sight of them again is rare.
1476.nuance: A plain account of the alchemist's confidence trick: the fee demanded in advance (குருமுடிச்சு, the guru's bundle) and the flight. The verse treats வாதம் (alchemy) as it is practised, a fraud, and says nothing about whether transmutation is possible.

1477.reading: They show a yoga hall and rise and float upward; they quickly learn the eight siddhis as a trick and stretch up tall; then, seized by lust, caught in the urine-bag of women, they die in this wide world like men possessed by a ghoul.
1477.nuance: அட்டசித்து வித்தை (the eight siddhis as an art) is siddhi as performance. The verse's sequence, display then lust then death, makes the showman's downfall ordinary desire, and the coarse phrase for women is the poet's contempt for the fall, not for women as such (compare 1467).

1478.reading: So that onlookers will esteem them as eaters of kaya-kalpa, they do conjuring tricks everywhere, frauds and cheats; because they smoke ganja at set hours and eat opium straight, they roam the land like dogs, licking and sniffing.
1478.nuance: காயகாயம் is read as காயகற்பம், the body-preserving medicine of Siddha tradition; the verse says its claimants are kept going by hemp and opium instead. It is a witness to the drugs of the wandering ascetic, and treats the kaya-kalpa claim as a cover rather than denying the medicine.

1479.reading: Those who beat the drum through the town that 'the body is as unstable as a bubble on water' and wander as wastrels; saying 'look, I will make jnana-siddhi for you in glory', they go straight on to seize others' property at length.
1479.nuance: The preacher's text is true (the body is a bubble) and the preacher is a thief; the verse separates the saying from the sayer. ஞானசித்தி செய்வேன் is the sale of attainment for money.

1480.reading: Ochre, matted hair, water-pots, a seat, dangling rudraksha and the yoga staff: oxen who carry these, leaving the wife to drift, roam every land and, alas, wander begging a mouthful at every house, the sinners.
1480.nuance: The full kit of the Saiva yogi is listed and its bearers called மாடுகள், cattle. தேவியை அலையவிட்டு (leaving the wife to wander) is the specific charge, and with 1467 and 1470 it makes the renouncer's desertion of his household the fault, not his gear alone.

1481.reading: Those who say 'look, I will first grant siddhi here so you reach release', swear oaths everywhere and put on the swami's garb; to fatten the belly daily they talk of justice and knowledge and, as devotion, snatch money: they fall into the waste hell.
1481.nuance: நித்தியம் வயிறு வளர்க்க (to grow the belly daily) is the motive the verse assigns to the whole trade of religious teaching for money. The promise sold is the double one, siddhi now and mukti after.

1482.reading: In fine red wood you carve the heads of images; from a branch without a knot you make foot-sandals and destroy it; if you could seek and look at the one who shines within you, this mala, the three malas and any mala whatever would be no more.
1482.nuance: The carpenter makes gods and sandals from the same tree, which is the argument against the carved god. The last line's இம்மலமும் மும்மலமும் எம்மலமும் piles up the Siddhanta term for the soul's impurities and says all vanish on seeing within.

1483.reading: Running in every direction and everywhere, plunging the head in countless rivers, will they become pure jnanis? Sinners who do not bow with devotion to Hara's feet will sink without release in the waste hell, grieving and wandering.
1483.nuance: The alternative to river-bathing is not a yogic technique here but பத்தி, bowing to Hara's feet; the chapter's positive note is devotional as often as it is gnostic.

1484.reading: If one fashions the varied forms of mighty gods in stone, silver, copper, iron or dried plates and praises them, does it give the great bliss, the place where troubles end? Say! No, no, no, no, by the Lord's oath, no.
1484.nuance: The four-fold இல்லை and the oath (ஈசன் ஆணை) make this the chapter's flattest denial. தராக்கள் is unclear, perhaps plates or dried clay. The verse answers 1472's list of cheap materials with the costly ones, so that price makes no difference.

1485.reading: This world was born in the Lord's five letters; the moving and the unmoving dwell gloriously in the five letters; the many exalted lives rise in the five letters; certain, true awakening of knowledge stands in the five letters.
1485.nuance: Four lines, four claims, each ending in ஐந்தெழுத்திலே: cosmogony, ontology, life and knowledge all placed in the five letters. After the chapter's destruction of outward forms this is the one form left standing, and 1488 shows how it is to be used.

1486.reading: Because staring and staring at shastras one goes blind, fools praise the sun straight on until their eyes fail; if you can know the fit vessel and practise silent devotion, by that rule all become pure, just so.
1486.nuance: Two kinds of blinding are paired, by books and by sun-worship. பாத்திரம் அறிந்து may mean knowing the fit recipient of devotion, or oneself as the vessel; சூத்திரப்படி may be 'by that rule' or, with the puppet-string sense of சூத்திரம், 'as moved by that string'. மோன பக்தி (silent devotion) is the verse's positive term.

1487.reading: Cattle with no firmness of mind, dull and tethered, who in anger gather up others' property and hoard it, and who day after day roam every town for their food: these are the joyless sinners whom many in their own kind revile.
1487.nuance: The verse joins theft and begging in one figure: the hoarder who still wanders for meals. மனவுறுதி இல்லாத (without steadiness of mind) is the diagnosis, which makes greed a failure of mind rather than a sin of the hand.

1488.reading: Chant 'Sivaayavasi' and this whole world is yours; chant 'Sivaayavasi' and everything is attainment; chant 'Sivaayavasi' and you may rule the sky; 'Sivaayavasi' itself becomes the fire with two heads.
1488.nuance: சிவாயவசி rearranges the five letters சி வா ய ந ம so that they end in வசி, which tradition reads as வாசி, the breath: the mantra is to be chanted on the breath. இருதலைத்தீ (two-headed fire) may be the breath burning at both nostrils, or the fire that burns both good and bad deeds. The closing verse of the work promises what the chapter has mocked when sold: the world, siddhi, the sky.

links.note: Tirumular says that though one recites the Vedas and Agamas, what is ours lies in one letter of the Lord; Sivavakkiyar says the labour of reciting the Vedas is wasted while the Lord is within. Tirumular still keeps a letter to master; Sivavakkiyar keeps only the inward look, though 1485 and 1488 give him the five letters too.

The Kural says that as this world is not for those without wealth, that world is not for those without அருள்; Sivavakkiyar says that where there are hands and wealth and no அருள், there is no Supreme, only a waste hell. Both make compassion, not rite, the condition of the beyond, and both set it against பொருள்.

Arunagirinathar describes lovemaking and asks to see clearly how to leave that embrace for Murugan's feet; Sivavakkiyar says no god has not joined a woman's shoulder and that human life flourishes in that union. The conflict holds on whether union with a woman is an obstacle to the way; Arunagiri's plea assumes it is, Sivavakkiyar's verse denies it.

Tirumular says Siva-gnanis wander as men dead while body and senses remain; Sivavakkiyar says people count the siddhar mad because heaven and earth are one to him. Both describe how the knower looks to those who cannot read him.

The Kural says one who tends the departing guest and watches for the next will be a good guest to the gods; Sivavakkiyar says the guest who comes becomes the Lord and grants life. Both make hospitality a path to the divine, the Kural by reward, the Siddhar by identity.
Tirumular asks whether wasting oneself away is tapas; Sivavakkiyar tells the hermits chewing dry leaves that their body wastes and anxiety grows. Both deny that self-starvation is austerity.

Arunagirinathar asks not to wander the earth in ochre, enter forests and punish the body, but to be given Murugan's feet; Sivavakkiyar asks whether those who leave their land to clear forests and hills will see the Lord's feet, and answers that none has gained release that way.

Tirumular makes the earth the base, the sky the linga, the sea its bathing hall and the directions its garment; Sivavakkiyar says that after wood, stone, turmeric, cloth and dung there is no god but the open space. Both replace the made image with the cosmos, though Tirumular keeps the linga's form and Sivavakkiyar keeps none.

The Kural says not killing one creature to eat is better than a thousand sacrifices with oblations; Sivavakkiyar says the goat and cock offered at the Pidari shrine do not cure, since the deity is not the cause. The Kural's ground is non-killing, the Siddhar's is futility, but both set aside blood sacrifice.

The Kural's hidden conduct is a hunter in a bush snaring birds under cover of austerity; Sivavakkiyar's pious thieves make puja and vows flourish while seizing others' property. Both describe religion used as a blind for predation.

The Kural's hypocrite is red as the kunri seed outside and black at the tip; Sivavakkiyar's is white with ash outside and a liar within, his ash the dust where a donkey rolled. Both are judgements of the outward sign by the inner fault.

Tirumular says that by chanting the five letters, through grace, copper becomes gold; Sivavakkiyar describes the man who promises to make gold and runs off with the fee. Sivavakkiyar does not deny transmutation, but his verse makes the alchemist's promise the mark of a fraud, which narrows what Tirumular's line can be taken to license.

Tirumular says the eight siddhis come through eightfold yoga by mastering the breath; Sivavakkiyar describes men who learn the eight siddhis as a stage trick, float upward for show, fall to lust and die. The powers are real for both; Sivavakkiyar's verse says they can be counterfeited and that display is the sign of counterfeit.

The Naladiyar's sages who see the body as a bubble in rain and resolve to end their wandering are the model; Sivavakkiyar's drummers who preach that the body is a bubble and then rob their hearers are the parody. The same image is held sincerely in one text and sold in the other.

Tirumular lists earrings, rudraksha, bowl, seat, yoga band and staff as the ten emblems of the yogi; Sivavakkiyar lists ochre, matted hair, pots, seat, rudraksha and staff and calls their bearers oxen who desert their wives to beg. The conflict holds if Sivavakkiyar condemns the garb as such; if his target is only those who use it to abandon a household and beg, it is a qualification, and Tirumular's own chapter on false garb (1655 to 1660) agrees with him.

The Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; Sivavakkiyar's matted-haired, ochre-robed men have kept the hair and not given up the fault. Both deny the outward mark any weight.
Tirumular says the false garb is worn for the sake of eating; Sivavakkiyar says the swami's garb is put on to fatten the belly daily. The motive assigned to false renunciation is the same in both.

The Kural says outer purity comes by water and inner purity is seen through truth; Sivavakkiyar asks whether plunging the head in countless rivers makes a pure jnani and answers that devotion does. Both deny water the power to make the inner clean.

Tirumular says that by the five letters the Lord made the five elements and the many wombs of birth and bears the world; Sivavakkiyar says the world was born, the moving and unmoving dwell and lives rise in the five letters. The cosmogony of the five letters is the same in both texts.

Tirumular's chakra chapter gives further orders of the five letters ending in a form beginning வசி; Sivavakkiyar's closing verse chants சிவாயவசி, the five letters reordered to end in வசி. Both texts permute the pancakshara to bring out the வசி/வாசி, read by tradition as the breath, and both attach power to the permuted form.

new_concepts.gloss: the breath worked as a practice; the Siddhars' word for breath control
new_concepts.label_source: Also declared in ch073; here hidden in the mantra form சிவாயவசி of 1488

new_concepts.gloss: alchemy: the claimed transmutation of base metals to silver and gold
new_concepts.label_source: 1476 uses வாதம் (வாதம்செய்வேன்) in this sense; the full word இரசவாதம் is the common name

source_issues: 1469: an editor's gloss line (மன்று - மன்றம்; சபை; விமலன் - மலமற்றவன்) has been printed as a fifth line of the verse text, and the GLOSSES entry attached to 1469 (சருகு) belongs to 1470.
1473 line 3 (நங்கச்சொல்லு நலிமிகுந்து ... மூஞ்சூராய்) is hard to construe and may be corrupt.
1478 line 1 காயகாயம் is probably a corruption of காயகற்பம்.
1480 line 4 ends அலைவரை where the sense wants அலைவரே, probably a copying slip.
